entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5439"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 42</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.42.1-Job.42.6">Job 42:1-6</reference>. Job's Penitent Reply.</title> <div sID="gen8191" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5439"/>2. In the first clause he owns God to be omnipotent over nature, as contrasted with his own feebleness, which God had proved (<reference osisRef="Job.40.15">Job 40:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.41.34">41:34</reference>); in the second, that God is supremely just (which, in order to be governor of the world, He must needs be) in all His dealings, as contrasted with his own vileness (<reference osisRef="Job.42.6">Job 42:6</reference>), and incompetence to deal with the wicked as a just judge (<reference osisRef="Job.40.8-Job.40.14">Job 40:8-14</reference>).<div eID="gen8191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8192" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thought--</hi>"purpose," as in <reference osisRef="Job.17.11">Job 17:11</reference>; but it is usually applied to evil devices (<reference osisRef="Job.21.27">Job 21:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.2">Psa 10:2</reference>): the ambiguous word is designedly chosen to express that, while to Job's finite view, God's plans seem bad, to the All-wise One they continue unhindered in their development, and will at last be seen to be as good as they are infinitely wise. No evil can emanate from the Parent of good (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.13">Jas 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">17</reference>); but it is His prerogative to overrule evil to good. <div eID="gen8192" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5440"/><div sID="gen8193" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5440"/>3. I am the man! Job in God's own words (<reference osisRef="Job.38.2">Job 38:2</reference>) expresses his deep and humble penitence. God's word concerning our guilt should be engraven on our hearts and form the groundwork of our confession. Most men in confessing sin palliate rather than confess. Job in omitting "by words" (<reference osisRef="Job.38.2">Job 38:2</reference>), goes even further than God's accusation. Not merely my words, but my whole thoughts and ways were "without knowledge."<div eID="gen8193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8194" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">too wonderful--</hi>I rashly denied that Thou hast any fixed plan in governing human affairs, merely because Thy plan was "too wonderful" for my comprehension. <div eID="gen8194" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5442"/><div sID="gen8196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5442"/><hi type="bold">5. hearing of the ear--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.18.44">Psa 18:44</reference>, Margin). Hearing and seeing are often in antithesis (<reference osisRef="Job.29.11">Job 29:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.8">Psa 18:8</reference>).<div eID="gen8196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8197" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seeth--</hi>not God's face (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.20">Ex 33:20</reference>), but His presence in the veil of a dark cloud (<reference osisRef="Job.38.1">Job 38:1</reference>). Job implies also that, besides this literal seeing, he now saw spiritually what he had indistinctly taken on hearsay before God's infinite wisdom. He "now" proves this; he had seen in a literal sense before, at the beginning of God's speech, but he had not seen spiritually till "now" at its close. <div eID="gen8197" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5444"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.42.7-Job.42.17">Job 42:7-17</reference>. Epilogue, in prose.</title> <div sID="gen8199" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5444"/><hi type="bold">7. to Eliphaz--</hi>because he was the foremost of the three friends; their speeches were but the echo of his.<div eID="gen8199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8200" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">right--</hi>literally, "well-grounded," sure and true. Their spirit towards Job was unkindly, and to justify themselves in their unkindliness they used false arguments (<reference osisRef="Job.13.7">Job 13:7</reference>); (namely, that calamities always prove peculiar guilt); therefore, though it was "for God" they spake thus falsely, God "reproves" them, as Job said He would (<reference osisRef="Job.13.10">Job 13:10</reference>).<div eID="gen8200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8201" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ... Job hath--</hi>Job had spoken rightly in relation to them and their argument, denying their theory, and the fact which they alleged, that he was peculiarly guilty and a hypocrite; but wrongly in relation to God, when he fell into the opposite extreme of almost denying all guilt. This extreme he has now repented of, and therefore God speaks of him as now altogether "right." <div eID="gen8201" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: Job 42:7-17 . Their spirit towards Job was unkindly, and to justify themselves in their unkindliness they used false arguments ( Job 13:7 ); (namely, that calamities always prove peculiar guilt); therefore, though it was "for God" they spake thus falsely, God "reproves" them, as Job said He would ( Job 13:10 ). as ... Job hath-- Job had spoken rightly in relation to them and their argument, denying their theory, and the fact which they alleged, that he was peculiarly guilty and a hypocrite; but wrongly in relation to God, when he fell into the opposite extreme of almost denying all guilt. This extreme he has now repented of, and therefore God speaks of him as now altogether "right."

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5445"/><div sID="gen8202" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5445"/><hi type="bold">8. seven--</hi>(See Introduction). The number offered by the Gentile prophet (<reference osisRef="Num.23.1">Nu 23:1</reference>). Job plainly lived before the legal priesthood, &c. The patriarchs acted as priests for their families; and sometimes as praying mediators (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.17">Ge 20:17</reference>), thus foreshadowing the true Mediator (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">1Ti 2:5</reference>), but sacrifice accompanies and is the groundwork on which the mediation rests.<div eID="gen8202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8203" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him--</hi>rather, "His person [face] only" (see on <reference osisRef="Job.22.30">Job 22:30</reference>). The "person," must be first accepted, before God can accept his offering and work (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.4">Ge 4:4</reference>); that can be only through Jesus Christ.<div eID="gen8203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">folly--</hi>impiety (<reference osisRef="Job.1.22">Job 1:22</reference>; 2:10). <div eID="gen8204" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 8. seven-- (See Introduction). The number offered by the Gentile prophet ( Nu 23:1 ). Job plainly lived before the legal priesthood, &c. The patriarchs acted as priests for their families; and sometimes as praying mediators ( Ge 20:17 ), thus foreshadowing the true Mediator ( 1Ti 2:5 ), but sacrifice accompanies and is the groundwork on which the mediation rests. him-- rather, "His person [face] only" (see on Job 22:30 ). The "person," must be first accepted, before God can accept his offering and work ( Ge 4:4 ); that can be only through Jesus Christ. folly-- impiety ( Job 1:22 ; 2:10).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5447"/><div sID="gen8206" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5447"/><hi type="bold">10. turned ... captivity--</hi>proverbial for restored, or amply indemnified him for all he had lost (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.53">Eze 16:53</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">Psa 14:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.11">Ho 6:11</reference>). Thus the future vindication of man, body and soul, against Satan (<reference osisRef="Job.1.9-Job.1.12">Job 1:9-12</reference>), at the resurrection (<reference osisRef="Job.19.25-Job.19.27">Job 19:25-27</reference>), has its earnest and adumbration in the temporal vindication of Job at last by Jehovah in person.<div eID="gen8206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8207" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">twice--</hi>so to the afflicted literal and spiritual Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Is 40:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.7">60:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">61:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.12">Zec 9:12</reference>). As in Job's case, so in that of Jesus Christ, the glorious recompense follows the "intercession" for enemies (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Is 53:12</reference>). <div eID="gen8207" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 10. turned ... captivity-- proverbial for restored, or amply indemnified him for all he had lost ( Eze 16:53 ; Psa 14:7 ; Ho 6:11 ). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5448"/><div sID="gen8208" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5448"/>11. It was Job's complaint in his misery that his "brethren," were "estranged" from him (<reference osisRef="Job.19.13">Job 19:13</reference>); these now return with the return of his prosperity (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.20">Pr 14:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.6">19:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.7">7</reference>); the true friend loveth at all times (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">Pr 17:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.18.24">18:24</reference>). "Swallow friends leave in the winter and return with the spring" [Henry].<div eID="gen8208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8209" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eat bread--</hi>in token of friendship (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.9">Psa 41:9</reference>).<div eID="gen8209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8210" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">piece of money--</hi>Presents are usual in visiting a man of rank in the East, especially after a calamity (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.23">2Ch 32:23</reference>). Hebrew, kesita. Magee translates "a lamb" (the medium of exchange then before money was used), as it is in Margin of <reference osisRef="Gen.33.19">Ge 33:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.24.32">Jos 24:32</reference>. But it is from the Arabic kasat, "weighed out" [Umbreit], not coined; so <reference osisRef="Gen.42.35">Ge 42:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.33.19">33:19</reference>; compare with <reference osisRef="Gen.23.15">Ge 23:15</reference>, makes it likely it was equal to four shekels; Hebrew kashat, "pure," namely, metal. The term, instead of the usual "shekel," &c., is a mark of antiquity.<div eID="gen8210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8211" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">earring--</hi>whether for the nose or ear (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.4">Ge 35:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.21">Is 3:21</reference>). Much of the gold in the East, in the absence of banks, is in the shape of ornaments. <div eID="gen8211" type="x-p"/>

Names significant of his restored prosperity (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.25">Ge 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.5.29">5:29</reference>).<div eID="gen8214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jemima--</hi>"daylight," after his "night" of calamity; but Maurer, "a dove."<div eID="gen8215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Kezia--</hi>"cassia," an aromatic herb (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.8">Psa 45:8</reference>), instead of his offensive breath and ulcers.<div eID="gen8216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Keren-happuch--</hi>"horn of stibium," a paint with which females dyed their eyelids; in contrast to his "horn defiled in the dust" (<reference osisRef="Job.16.15">Job 16:15</reference>). entries.content_plain: 14. Names significant of his restored prosperity ( Ge 4:25 ; 5:29 ). Jemima-- "daylight," after his "night" of calamity; but Maurer, "a dove." Kezia-- "cassia," an aromatic herb ( Psa 45:8 ), instead of his offensive breath and ulcers. Keren-happuch-- "horn of stibium," a paint with which females dyed their eyelids; in contrast to his "horn defiled in the dust" ( Job 16:15 ). The names also imply the beauty of his daughters.

Keren-happuch-- "horn of stibium," a paint with which females dyed their eyelids; in contrast to his "horn defiled in the dust" ( Job 16:15 ). The names also imply the beauty of his daughters.

The Septuagint makes Job live a hundred seventy years after his calamity, and two hundred forty in all. This would make him seventy at the time of his calamity, which added to a hundred forty in Hebrew text makes up two hundred ten; a little more than the age (two hundred five) of Terah, father of Abraham, perhaps his contemporary. entries.content_plain: 17. full of days-- fully sated and contented with all the happiness that life could give him; realizing what Eliphaz had painted as the lot of the godly ( Job 5:26 ; Psa 91:16 ; Ge 25:8 ; 35:29 ).
